books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

stimulus.text:
“The conditions which surround us best justify our co-operation; we meet in the midst of a nation brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin. Corruption dominates the ballot-box, the Legislatures, the Congress, and touches even the ermine of the bench. The people are demoralized; most of the States have been compelled to isolate the voters at the polling places to prevent universal intimidation and bribery. The newspapers are largely subsidized or muzzled, public opinion silenced, business prostrated, homes covered with mortgages, labor impoverished, and the land concentrating in the hands of capitalists. The urban workmen are denied the right to organize for self-protection, imported pauperized labor beats down their wages, a hireling standing army, unrecognized by our laws, is established to shoot them down, and they are rapidly degenerating into European conditions. The fruits of the toil of millions are boldly stolen to build up colossal fortunes for a few, unprecedented in the history of mankind; and the possessors of those, in turn, despise the Republic and endanger liberty. From the same prolific womb of governmental injustice we breed the two great classes—tramps and millionaires.”

“We believe that the power of government—in other words, of the people—should be expanded (as in the case of the postal service) as rapidly and as far as the good sense of an intelligent people and the teachings of experience shall justify, to the end that oppression, injustice, and poverty shall eventually cease in the land.”

(People’s Party, Omaha Platform, July 4, 1892)
stimulus.source_note: People’s (Populist) Party, Omaha Platform, July 4, 1892, Preamble. Public domain; wording checked against the text in Edward McPherson, A Handbook of Politics for 1892, as reproduced by LibreTexts and the American Presidency Project.

stem: The preamble’s claim that the nation breeds “tramp” and “millionaire” best supports which conclusion about the Populists’ view of government?

options.text: Government should leave the economy entirely alone
options.misconception: The preamble calls for government power to expand, not to withdraw.

options.text: Only state governments should regulate railroads and banks
options.misconception: The preamble looks to national government power, not to the states alone.

options.text: Government injustice had created two extremes of wealth and poverty
Farmers and workers had grown rich from government aid
options.misconception: The preamble says the fruits of labor were stolen to build fortunes for a few.

rationales.A: The closing lines call for the power of government to expand, the opposite of leaving the economy alone.
rationales.B: Nothing in the passage assigns the remedy to the states alone.
rationales.C: The two classes breed from the same womb of governmental injustice, so government made both extremes.
rationales.D: Farmers and workers are the ones robbed, not enriched, in the preamble’s account.
rationales.general:
Unpack the metaphor the Populists chose.
1. The preamble says the fruits of millions are stolen to build colossal fortunes for a few.
2. From the same womb of governmental injustice come tramps and millionaires.
3. Both extremes share one parent: government that serves the wealthy.
4. The Populists blamed government itself for making rich and poor alike.
Remember: when a source names one parent for two opposites, it blames that parent for both.
